title: Run it yourself
text: Every page on this site is built from notebooks you can run on your own CUDA GPU.

title: Run it yourself
text:
Requirements

Linux with an NVIDIA GPU and a recent driver (tested: driver 580, CUDA 13.0)
juliaup (the project pins Julia 1.12)
uv for the Python/JAX environment
Quarto ≥ 1.10
make

title: Run it yourself
text:
Install
git clone https://github.com/michel2323/WEANJ
cd WEANJ
make setup
make setup installs the Julia 1.12 channel, instantiates and precompiles the Julia environment in julia/ (Enzyme, Reactant, CUDA), creates the Python environment in python/ (JAX with CUDA 13), and writes _environment.local so Quarto uses that Python. The first run downloads several GB and takes 10–15 minutes.

title: Run it yourself
text:
Check the toolchain
quarto render smoke/
This runs a tiny gradient on the GPU with each of the three tools. Open _site/smoke/index.html; all three tabs should show output.

title: Run it yourself
text:
Run the examples
quarto preview                      # browse the site, edit and re-run notebooks live
quarto render examples/01-particles/enzyme.qmd   # re-run one notebook
make run-gpu                        # re-run everything; refreshes _freeze/ and benchmarks/
Rendering a single notebook always executes it. Rendering the whole site uses the frozen outputs in _freeze/, so it does not need a GPU.

title: Run it yourself
text:
Troubleshooting

JAX prints CUDA_ERROR_OUT_OF_MEMORY

Another process is using the GPU. The notebooks disable JAX’s up-front memory reservation, but benchmark numbers are only meaningful on an idle GPU: make gpu-check lists what is running.

Julia version mismatch

The notebooks start Julia with julia +1.12. Run juliaup add 1.12.

title: Why Enzyme and not JAX?
text:
Note



Work in progress. The examples are being added one at a time; see the project plan.
“Why do you use Julia instead of JAX?” is a fair question, and “JAX can’t sort” is the wrong answer: jax.lax.sort is differentiable. The real difference is the execution model.
JAX differentiates pure functions over fixed-shape arrays with a static computation graph. Anything that fits that model runs well, often better than hand-written code, because XLA fuses and vectorises it. Enzyme differentiates the imperative program as written, including in-place mutation, data-dependent loop bounds and growing buffers. When an algorithm’s efficient form is irregular, JAX makes you regularise it with padding, masks, static trip counts or implicit differentiation. Enzyme lets you keep it.
Each example below implements the same loss three times, with Enzyme.jl, with Reactant.jl, and with JAX, checks that all three give the same gradient, and times them on a CUDA GPU. Reactant is the control: it is Julia compiled through XLA, the same static-graph model as JAX. Where Reactant hits the same wall as JAX, the cause is the execution model, not the language.

title: Why Enzyme and not JAX?
text:
Where the gap shows up

Data-dependent output size or sparsity

Compaction and filtering (x[mask], push!), sparse assembly with data-dependent fill-in, contact detection, tree codes (octrees, Barnes–Hut). JAX needs a static upper bound and masks.

Data-dependent control flow

Iterative solvers with convergence tests, adaptive time stepping. JAX cannot reverse-differentiate lax.while_loop, so you fix the iteration count or switch to implicit differentiation.

Sequential in-place updates

Gauss–Seidel, SOR, Thomas algorithm, sweeps where element i depends on the just-updated i−1. In JAX these become lax.scan with the whole array as carry, and reverse mode stores every carry unless you rematerialise.

Irregular neighbour access

Particle methods with cell lists (sort by cell, loop over a data-dependent number of neighbours), scatter-accumulate with data-dependent indices, histogramming, resampling.

title: Why Enzyme and not JAX?
text:
Where JAX wins
Dense, batched, regular work: most of machine learning, many PDE stencils, anything whose naive cost already equals its smart cost. There the regularised JAX version is often faster despite padding, because XLA fuses and the hardware wants regular access. And the advantage on this site is Enzyme’s, not Julia’s: Julia AD tools that do not support mutation (Zygote) cannot do this either.

title: 01. Particles — JAX
text:
import math
import numpy as np
import weanj  # sets XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_PREALLOCATE=false before JAX initialises
import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp
from jax_md import partition, space

jax.config.update("jax_enable_x64", True)
EXAMPLE = "01-particles"
x0 = jnp.asarray(weanj.load_inputs(EXAMPLE)["x"].T)  # (N, 2); Julia stores 2×N


# Idiomatic JAX: jax-md's neighbour list. It is a fixed-capacity padded pair list;
# `allocate` (outside jit) sizes it from the data, `update` (inside jit) refills it,
# and `did_buffer_overflow` must be checked after every call.
NUMBER_DENSITY, H, MASS = 10.0, 0.5, 1.0
RC, RHO0 = 2 * H, NUMBER_DENSITY

def box_size(n):
    return math.sqrt(n / NUMBER_DENSITY)

def W(r, h=H):
    """2D cubic spline. No `if`: both branches are evaluated and selected."""
    q = r / h
    sigma = 10.0 / (7.0 * math.pi * h * h)
    t = jnp.maximum(2.0 - q, 0.0)
    return sigma * jnp.where(q < 1.0, 1.0 - 1.5 * q**2 + 0.75 * q**3, 0.25 * t**3)

def make_loss(n, displacement):
    w0 = MASS * float(W(0.0))  # self-contribution; jax-md's pair list excludes i == j

    def loss(x, nbrs):
        nbrs = nbrs.update(x)  # rebuild the cell list from the current positions
        i, j = nbrs.idx
        mask = i < n  # padded slots hold index n
        dR = jax.vmap(displacement)(x[i], x[j])
        dR = jnp.where(mask[:, None], dR, 1.0)  # padded dR = 0 would make ∇‖dR‖ NaN
        r = jnp.sqrt(jnp.sum(dR**2, axis=1))
        w = jnp.where(mask, MASS * W(r), 0.0)
        rho = w0 + jax.ops.segment_sum(w, i, num_segments=n)
        return jnp.sum((rho - RHO0) ** 2), nbrs

    return loss

class Particles:
    """Jitted loss and gradient with jax-md's overflow-and-reallocate protocol."""

    def __init__(self, x, capacity_multiplier=1.25):
        self.n = x.shape[0]
        L = box_size(self.n)
        displacement, _ = space.periodic(L)
        self.neighbor_fn = partition.neighbor_list(
            displacement, L, RC, dr_threshold=0.0,
            capacity_multiplier=capacity_multiplier, format=partition.Sparse)
        self.nbrs = self.neighbor_fn.allocate(x)
        loss = make_loss(self.n, displacement)
        self._loss = jax.jit(loss)
        self._grad = jax.jit(jax.grad(loss, has_aux=True))

    def _checked(self, f, x):
        out, nbrs = f(x, self.nbrs)
        if nbrs.did_buffer_overflow:  # host sync, as in jax-md's examples
            self.nbrs = self.neighbor_fn.allocate(x)
            out, nbrs = f(x, self.nbrs)
        self.nbrs = nbrs
        return out

    def loss(self, x):
        return self._checked(self._loss, x)

    def grad(self, x):
        return self._checked(self._grad, x)


P0 = Particles(x0)
g = P0.grad(x0)
print(f"loss = {float(P0.loss(x0)):.10f}   ‖∇loss‖ = {float(jnp.linalg.norm(g)):.6f}")

loss = 12476.3617428792   ‖∇loss‖ = 7526.066606



err = weanj.fd_check(lambda y: P0.loss(jnp.asarray(y)), np.asarray(x0), np.asarray(g), n=10)
weanj.save_gradient(EXAMPLE, "jax", np.asarray(g).T)  # back to Julia's 2×N layout
print(f"finite differences: max rel. error {err:.1e} on 10 components")

finite differences: max rel. error 5.0e-08 on 10 components



import time

def positions(n, seed=1):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    return (rng.random((n, 2)) * box_size(n)).astype(np.float32)

Ns = [10**3, 10**4, 10**5, 10**6]
for device in ("cpu", "gpu"):
    records = []
    with jax.default_device(jax.devices(device)[0]):
        for N in Ns:
            x = jnp.asarray(positions(N))
            t0 = time.perf_counter()
            P = Particles(x)
            jax.block_until_ready(P.grad(x))
            compile_s = time.perf_counter() - t0
            samples = 3 if N >= 10**5 else 10
            records.append(dict(
                dtype="Float32", N=N,
                forward_s=weanj.time_median(lambda: P.loss(x), sync=jax.block_until_ready, samples=samples),
                grad_s=weanj.time_median(lambda: P.grad(x), sync=jax.block_until_ready, samples=samples),
                compile_s=compile_s, peak_mem_bytes=None,
                slots=int(P.nbrs.idx.shape[1])))
    weanj.write_results(EXAMPLE, "jax", device, records)
    for r in records:
        print(f"{device}  N={r['N']:<8d} forward {1e3*r['forward_s']:9.3f} ms   "
              f"gradient {1e3*r['grad_s']:9.3f} ms   compile {r['compile_s']:5.1f} s")

title: 01. Particles — Enzyme.jl
text:
using WEANJ, Enzyme, CUDA, KernelAbstractions, Printf
include("common.jl")   # Params, kernel W, minimum image, inputs

# Enzyme's reverse-mode GPU kernels store per-iteration values of data-dependent
# loops in device `malloc` memory. CUDA's default device heap is 8 MB, which overflows
# above ~30k particles (illegal memory access). Must be set before the first kernel.
CUDA.limit!(CUDA.LIMIT_MALLOC_HEAP_SIZE, 2^31)

x0 = ensure_inputs()["x"]    # shared Float64 correctness input, 2×1000
p0 = Params(size(x0, 2))

Params{Float64}(10.0, 0.5, 1.0, 10.0, 10)



# The whole pipeline is differentiated: cell ids, counting sort, gather into sorted
# order, and neighbour loops whose ranges depend on the data.
function sph_loss(x::AbstractMatrix{T}, p::Params{T}) where {T}
    N, nc = size(x, 2), p.nc
    s, rc = p.L / nc, 2 * p.h

    # 1. cell id of every particle, and particles per cell
    cell  = Vector{Int}(undef, N)
    start = zeros(Int, nc * nc + 1)
    @inbounds for i in 1:N
        cx = mod(floor(Int, x[1, i] / s), nc)
        cy = mod(floor(Int, x[2, i] / s), nc)
        cell[i] = 1 + cx + nc * cy
        start[cell[i] + 1] += 1
    end

    # 2. counting sort by cell: start[c] is the first sorted index of cell c
    start[1] = 1
    for c in 1:nc * nc
        start[c + 1] += start[c]
    end
    cursor = start[1:end-1]
    perm = Vector{Int}(undef, N)
    @inbounds for i in 1:N
        perm[cursor[cell[i]]] = i
        cursor[cell[i]] += 1
    end

    # 3. gather positions into sorted order: each cell is contiguous in memory
    xs = similar(x)
    @inbounds for k in 1:N
        xs[1, k] = x[1, perm[k]]
        xs[2, k] = x[2, perm[k]]
    end

    # 4. density and loss over the 3×3 neighbouring cells; each cell is the range
    #    start[c]:start[c+1]-1, whose length depends on the data
    loss = zero(T)
    @inbounds for k in 1:N
        c = cell[perm[k]] - 1
        cx, cy = c % nc, c ÷ nc
        ρ = zero(T)
        for dy in -1:1, dx in -1:1
            cn = 1 + mod(cx + dx, nc) + nc * mod(cy + dy, nc)
            for l in start[cn]:start[cn + 1] - 1
                rx = minimg(xs[1, k] - xs[1, l], p.L)
                ry = minimg(xs[2, k] - xs[2, l], p.L)
                r2 = rx * rx + ry * ry
                if r2 < rc * rc
                    ρ += p.m * W(sqrt(r2), p.h)
                end
            end
        end
        loss += (ρ - p.ρ0)^2
    end
    return loss
end

sph_loss (generic function with 1 method)



function sph_gradient(x::Matrix{T}, p::Params{T}) where {T}
    dx = zero(x)
    Enzyme.autodiff(Reverse, sph_loss, Active, Duplicated(x, dx), Const(p))
    return dx
end

g_cpu = sph_gradient(x0, p0)
@printf "loss = %.10f   ‖∇loss‖ = %.6f\n" sph_loss(x0, p0) sqrt(sum(abs2, g_cpu))

loss = 12476.3617428793   ‖∇loss‖ = 7526.066606



# Same algorithm as KernelAbstractions kernels. The cell list is integer-valued (zero
# derivative), so it is built outside the differentiated function with CUDA.jl's sort.
# The gather and the neighbour loops are differentiated.

# Box size, smoothing length etc. are not differentiated; declaring that lets Params be
# passed to GPU kernels, which reject active (differentiable) scalar arguments.
Enzyme.EnzymeRules.inactive_type(::Type{<:Params}) = true

@kernel function cell_ids!(cell, counts, @Const(x), s, nc)
    i = @index(Global)
    @inbounds begin
        cx = mod(unsafe_trunc(Int32, floor(x[1, i] / s)), Int32(nc))
        cy = mod(unsafe_trunc(Int32, floor(x[2, i] / s)), Int32(nc))
        cell[i] = Int32(1) + cx + Int32(nc) * cy
        KernelAbstractions.@atomic counts[cell[i] + 1] += Int32(1)
    end
end

function build_cells(x::CuMatrix{T}, p::Params{T}) where {T}
    N, nc = size(x, 2), p.nc
    cell = CuVector{Int32}(undef, N)
    counts = CUDA.zeros(Int32, nc * nc + 1)
    cell_ids!(get_backend(x))(cell, counts, x, p.L / nc, nc; ndrange=N)
    counts[1:1] .= 1
    perm = sortperm(cell)
    return (; perm=Int32.(perm), cell=cell[perm], start=cumsum(counts))
end

@kernel function gather!(xs, @Const(x), @Const(perm))
    k = @index(Global)
    @inbounds xs[1, k] = x[1, perm[k]]
    @inbounds xs[2, k] = x[2, perm[k]]
end

@kernel function density_loss!(e, @Const(xs), @Const(cellk), @Const(start), p)
    k = @index(Global)
    T, nc = eltype(xs), Int32(p.nc)
    @inbounds begin
        c = cellk[k] - Int32(1)
        cx, cy = c % nc, c ÷ nc
        ρ = zero(T)
        for dy in Int32(-1):Int32(1), dx in Int32(-1):Int32(1)
            cn = Int32(1) + mod(cx + dx, nc) + nc * mod(cy + dy, nc)
            for l in start[cn]:start[cn + 1] - Int32(1)      # data-dependent range
                rx = minimg(xs[1, k] - xs[1, l], p.L)
                ry = minimg(xs[2, k] - xs[2, l], p.L)
                r2 = rx * rx + ry * ry
                if r2 < 4 * p.h * p.h
                    ρ += p.m * W(sqrt(r2), p.h)
                end
            end
        end
        e[k] = (ρ - p.ρ0)^2
    end
end

"Per-particle loss terms e (in sorted order); the loss is sum(e)."
function sph_terms!(e, xs, x, cells, p)
    backend, N = get_backend(x), size(x, 2)
    gather!(backend)(xs, x, cells.perm; ndrange=N)
    density_loss!(backend)(e, xs, cells.cell, cells.start, p; ndrange=N)
    return nothing
end

function sph_loss(x::CuMatrix{T}, p::Params{T}) where {T}
    e, xs = similar(x, size(x, 2)), similar(x)
    sph_terms!(e, xs, x, build_cells(x, p), p)
    return sum(e)
end

sph_loss (generic function with 2 methods)



"Gradient of sum(e): reverse mode seeded with de = 1."
function sph_gradient(x::CuMatrix{T}, p::Params{T}) where {T}
    N = size(x, 2)
    e, de = similar(x, N), CUDA.ones(T, N)
    xs, dxs = similar(x), CUDA.zeros(T, size(x))
    dx = CUDA.zeros(T, size(x))
    Enzyme.autodiff(Reverse, sph_terms!, Const,
                    Duplicated(e, de), Duplicated(xs, dxs), Duplicated(x, dx),
                    Const(build_cells(x, p)), Const(p))
    return dx
end

g_gpu = Array(sph_gradient(CuArray(x0), p0))
@printf "max |∇_gpu − ∇_cpu| / max |∇_cpu| = %.1e\n" maximum(abs, g_gpu - g_cpu) / maximum(abs, g_cpu)

"Neighbour candidates visited: Σ over particles of the occupancy of its 3×3 cells."
function slots_visited(x, p)
    s, nc = p.L / p.nc, p.nc
    occ = zeros(Int, nc, nc)
    for i in axes(x, 2)
        occ[1 + mod(floor(Int, x[1, i] / s), nc), 1 + mod(floor(Int, x[2, i] / s), nc)] += 1
    end
    return sum(occ[i, j] * sum(occ[mod1(i + a, nc), mod1(j + b, nc)] for a in -1:1, b in -1:1)
               for i in 1:nc, j in 1:nc)
end

Ns = [10^3, 10^4, 10^5, 10^6]
gpu_sync = _ -> CUDA.synchronize()
records = Dict("cpu" => [], "gpu" => [])
for (device, prep, sync) in (("cpu", identity, identity), ("gpu", CuArray, gpu_sync))
    for (n, N) in enumerate(Ns)
        p = Params{Float32}(N)

        samples = N >= 10^5 ? 3 : 10

            grad_s    = time_median(() -> sph_gradient(x, p); sync, samples),
            compile_s, peak_mem_bytes = nothing,
            slots = slots_visited(Array(x), p)))
    end

end

title: 01. Particles: sort, cell lists, and data-dependent neighbour loops
text:
\(N\) particles in a periodic square box, each with an SPH density \[\rho_i = \sum_j m\, W(\lVert x_i - x_j\rVert, h),\] where \(W\) is the 2D cubic-spline kernel with support \(2h\), and the loss \[\mathcal{L}(x) = \sum_i (\rho_i - \rho_0)^2 .\] We want \(\nabla_x \mathcal{L}\), the gradient with respect to all particle positions. The box grows with \(N\) so every particle has about 31 neighbours.
This loss came up in a Slack discussion as “something JAX can’t do because it needs sort!”. That is not quite right: jax.lax.sort is differentiable. What matters is how the efficient algorithm works:

compute each particle’s cell (integer, zero derivative),
sort particles by cell so each cell is contiguous in memory,
for each particle, loop over the 3×3 neighbouring cells, each a range start[c]:start[c+1]-1 whose length depends on the data,
accumulate kernel-weighted contributions.

The gradient flows through the gather in step 2 (as a permutation) and through step 4. Steps 1–3 only decide which pairs interact.

title: 01. Particles: sort, cell lists, and data-dependent neighbour loops
text:
Code
The Enzyme version is the algorithm above as plain loops, differentiated as written: on the CPU the whole pipeline, including the counting sort, is inside autodiff. JAX and Reactant cannot express step 3 (a loop whose bounds come from the data), so they regularise it. JAX uses jax-md’s padded neighbour list; Reactant uses a padded cell list. Both must pick a capacity from the data and check for overflow.

Enzyme.jl (CPU)Enzyme.jl (GPU)Reactant.jlJAX




# The whole pipeline is differentiated: cell ids, counting sort, gather into sorted
# order, and neighbour loops whose ranges depend on the data.
function sph_loss(x::AbstractMatrix{T}, p::Params{T}) where {T}
    N, nc = size(x, 2), p.nc
    s, rc = p.L / nc, 2 * p.h

    # 1. cell id of every particle, and particles per cell
    cell  = Vector{Int}(undef, N)
    start = zeros(Int, nc * nc + 1)
    @inbounds for i in 1:N
        cx = mod(floor(Int, x[1, i] / s), nc)
        cy = mod(floor(Int, x[2, i] / s), nc)
        cell[i] = 1 + cx + nc * cy
        start[cell[i] + 1] += 1
    end

    # 2. counting sort by cell: start[c] is the first sorted index of cell c
    start[1] = 1
    for c in 1:nc * nc
        start[c + 1] += start[c]
    end
    cursor = start[1:end-1]
    perm = Vector{Int}(undef, N)
    @inbounds for i in 1:N
        perm[cursor[cell[i]]] = i
        cursor[cell[i]] += 1
    end

    # 3. gather positions into sorted order: each cell is contiguous in memory
    xs = similar(x)
    @inbounds for k in 1:N
        xs[1, k] = x[1, perm[k]]
        xs[2, k] = x[2, perm[k]]
    end

    # 4. density and loss over the 3×3 neighbouring cells; each cell is the range
    #    start[c]:start[c+1]-1, whose length depends on the data
    loss = zero(T)
    @inbounds for k in 1:N
        c = cell[perm[k]] - 1
        cx, cy = c % nc, c ÷ nc
        ρ = zero(T)
        for dy in -1:1, dx in -1:1
            cn = 1 + mod(cx + dx, nc) + nc * mod(cy + dy, nc)
            for l in start[cn]:start[cn + 1] - 1
                rx = minimg(xs[1, k] - xs[1, l], p.L)
                ry = minimg(xs[2, k] - xs[2, l], p.L)
                r2 = rx * rx + ry * ry
                if r2 < rc * rc
                    ρ += p.m * W(sqrt(r2), p.h)
                end
            end
        end
        loss += (ρ - p.ρ0)^2
    end
    return loss
end

function sph_gradient(x::Matrix{T}, p::Params{T}) where {T}

    Enzyme.autodiff(Reverse, sph_loss, Active, Duplicated(x, dx), Const(p))
    return dx
end

# Same algorithm as KernelAbstractions kernels. The cell list is integer-valued (zero
# derivative), so it is built outside the differentiated function with CUDA.jl's sort.
# The gather and the neighbour loops are differentiated.

# Box size, smoothing length etc. are not differentiated; declaring that lets Params be
# passed to GPU kernels, which reject active (differentiable) scalar arguments.
Enzyme.EnzymeRules.inactive_type(::Type{<:Params}) = true

@kernel function cell_ids!(cell, counts, @Const(x), s, nc)
    i = @index(Global)
    @inbounds begin
        cx = mod(unsafe_trunc(Int32, floor(x[1, i] / s)), Int32(nc))
        cy = mod(unsafe_trunc(Int32, floor(x[2, i] / s)), Int32(nc))
        cell[i] = Int32(1) + cx + Int32(nc) * cy
        KernelAbstractions.@atomic counts[cell[i] + 1] += Int32(1)
    end
end

function build_cells(x::CuMatrix{T}, p::Params{T}) where {T}
    N, nc = size(x, 2), p.nc
    cell = CuVector{Int32}(undef, N)
    counts = CUDA.zeros(Int32, nc * nc + 1)
    cell_ids!(get_backend(x))(cell, counts, x, p.L / nc, nc; ndrange=N)
    counts[1:1] .= 1
    perm = sortperm(cell)
    return (; perm=Int32.(perm), cell=cell[perm], start=cumsum(counts))
end

@kernel function gather!(xs, @Const(x), @Const(perm))
    k = @index(Global)
    @inbounds xs[1, k] = x[1, perm[k]]
    @inbounds xs[2, k] = x[2, perm[k]]
end

@kernel function density_loss!(e, @Const(xs), @Const(cellk), @Const(start), p)
    k = @index(Global)
    T, nc = eltype(xs), Int32(p.nc)
    @inbounds begin
        c = cellk[k] - Int32(1)
        cx, cy = c % nc, c ÷ nc
        ρ = zero(T)
        for dy in Int32(-1):Int32(1), dx in Int32(-1):Int32(1)
            cn = Int32(1) + mod(cx + dx, nc) + nc * mod(cy + dy, nc)
            for l in start[cn]:start[cn + 1] - Int32(1)      # data-dependent range
                rx = minimg(xs[1, k] - xs[1, l], p.L)
                ry = minimg(xs[2, k] - xs[2, l], p.L)
                r2 = rx * rx + ry * ry
                if r2 < 4 * p.h * p.h
                    ρ += p.m * W(sqrt(r2), p.h)
                end
            end
        end
        e[k] = (ρ - p.ρ0)^2
    end
end

"Per-particle loss terms e (in sorted order); the loss is sum(e)."
function sph_terms!(e, xs, x, cells, p)
    backend, N = get_backend(x), size(x, 2)
    gather!(backend)(xs, x, cells.perm; ndrange=N)
    density_loss!(backend)(e, xs, cells.cell, cells.start, p; ndrange=N)
    return nothing
end

function sph_loss(x::CuMatrix{T}, p::Params{T}) where {T}
    e, xs = similar(x, size(x, 2)), similar(x)
    sph_terms!(e, xs, x, build_cells(x, p), p)
    return sum(e)
end

sph_loss (generic function with 2 methods)





"Gradient of sum(e): reverse mode seeded with de = 1."
function sph_gradient(x::CuMatrix{T}, p::Params{T}) where {T}
    N = size(x, 2)
    e, de = similar(x, N), CUDA.ones(T, N)
    xs, dxs = similar(x), CUDA.zeros(T, size(x))
    dx = CUDA.zeros(T, size(x))
    Enzyme.autodiff(Reverse, sph_terms!, Const,
                    Duplicated(e, de), Duplicated(xs, dxs), Duplicated(x, dx),
                    Const(build_cells(x, p)), Const(p))
    return dx
end

# Reactant traces Julia array code into one XLA program, so it has JAX's constraints:
# static shapes, no data-dependent loop bounds, no branches on traced values. The cell
# list is regularised like a padded JAX cell list: every neighbour cell is read
# through `cap` slots and slots past the cell's end are masked.

# `W` from common.jl branches (`if q < 1`), which cannot be traced. Select instead,
# evaluating both polynomials for every pair, as JAX's `jnp.where` does.
@inline function W_select(r, h::T) where {T}
    q = r / h
    σ = T(10) / (T(7) * T(π) * h * h)
    t = max(2 - q, zero(T))
    return σ * ifelse(q < 1, 1 - T(1.5) * q * q + T(0.75) * q * q * q, T(0.25) * t * t * t)
end

"""
First sorted index of each cell, using only sorts and gathers: merge the sorted cell
ids (keys 2c) with one probe per cell (keys 2c−1); the rank of probe c, minus the
c−1 probes before it, is the start of cell c.
"""
function cell_starts(cs, ncells)
    N = length(cs)
    probes = 2 .* Int32.(1:ncells+1) .- Int32(1)
    order = sortperm(vcat(2 .* cs, Reactant.promote_to(typeof(cs), probes)))
    rank = sortperm(order)                       # inverse permutation
    return rank[N+1:end] .- Int32.(0:ncells)
end

function sph_loss_padded(x::AbstractMatrix, p::Params{T}, ::Val{cap}) where {T,cap}
    N, nc = size(x, 2), p.nc
    s = p.L / nc

    cell = Int32(1) .+ mod.(floor.(Int32, x[1, :] ./ s), Int32(nc)) .+
           Int32(nc) .* mod.(floor.(Int32, x[2, :] ./ s), Int32(nc))
    perm = sortperm(cell)
    cs = cell[perm]
    start = cell_starts(cs, nc * nc)
    xs, ys = x[1, perm], x[2, perm]
    cxs, cys = (cs .- Int32(1)) .% Int32(nc), (cs .- Int32(1)) .÷ Int32(nc)
    slots = reshape(Int32.(0:cap-1), cap, 1)

    ρ = zero(xs)
    for dy in -1:1, dx in -1:1                   # unrolled at trace time
        cn = Int32(1) .+ mod.(cxs .+ Int32(dx), Int32(nc)) .+
             Int32(nc) .* mod.(cys .+ Int32(dy), Int32(nc))
        idx = reshape(start[cn], 1, N) .+ slots                  # (cap, N) candidates
        valid = idx .< reshape(start[cn .+ Int32(1)], 1, N)
        l = clamp.(idx, Int32(1), Int32(N))
        rx = minimg.(reshape(xs, 1, N) .- xs[l], p.L)
        ry = minimg.(reshape(ys, 1, N) .- ys[l], p.L)
        r2 = rx .^ 2 .+ ry .^ 2
        inside = valid .& (r2 .< 4 * p.h * p.h)
        r = sqrt.(ifelse.(inside, r2, one(T)))  # keep sqrt' finite on masked slots
        ρ = ρ .+ vec(sum(ifelse.(inside, p.m .* W_select.(r, p.h), zero(T)); dims=1))
    end
    return sum((ρ .- p.ρ0) .^ 2)
end

"Capacity needed: the largest cell occupancy. Too small silently drops neighbours."
function max_occupancy(x, p)
    s, nc = p.L / p.nc, p.nc
    counts = zeros(Int, nc * nc)
    for i in axes(x, 2)
        counts[1 + mod(floor(Int, x[1, i] / s), nc) + nc * mod(floor(Int, x[2, i] / s), nc)] += 1
    end
    return maximum(counts)
end

# Idiomatic JAX: jax-md's neighbour list. It is a fixed-capacity padded pair list;
# `allocate` (outside jit) sizes it from the data, `update` (inside jit) refills it,
# and `did_buffer_overflow` must be checked after every call.
NUMBER_DENSITY, H, MASS = 10.0, 0.5, 1.0
RC, RHO0 = 2 * H, NUMBER_DENSITY

def box_size(n):
    return math.sqrt(n / NUMBER_DENSITY)

def W(r, h=H):
    """2D cubic spline. No `if`: both branches are evaluated and selected."""
    q = r / h
    sigma = 10.0 / (7.0 * math.pi * h * h)
    t = jnp.maximum(2.0 - q, 0.0)
    return sigma * jnp.where(q < 1.0, 1.0 - 1.5 * q**2 + 0.75 * q**3, 0.25 * t**3)

def make_loss(n, displacement):
    w0 = MASS * float(W(0.0))  # self-contribution; jax-md's pair list excludes i == j

    def loss(x, nbrs):
        nbrs = nbrs.update(x)  # rebuild the cell list from the current positions
        i, j = nbrs.idx
        mask = i < n  # padded slots hold index n
        dR = jax.vmap(displacement)(x[i], x[j])
        dR = jnp.where(mask[:, None], dR, 1.0)  # padded dR = 0 would make ∇‖dR‖ NaN
        r = jnp.sqrt(jnp.sum(dR**2, axis=1))
        w = jnp.where(mask, MASS * W(r), 0.0)
        rho = w0 + jax.ops.segment_sum(w, i, num_segments=n)
        return jnp.sum((rho - RHO0) ** 2), nbrs

    return loss

class Particles:
    """Jitted loss and gradient with jax-md's overflow-and-reallocate protocol."""

    def __init__(self, x, capacity_multiplier=1.25):
        self.n = x.shape[0]
        L = box_size(self.n)
        displacement, _ = space.periodic(L)
        self.neighbor_fn = partition.neighbor_list(
            displacement, L, RC, dr_threshold=0.0,
            capacity_multiplier=capacity_multiplier, format=partition.Sparse)
        self.nbrs = self.neighbor_fn.allocate(x)
        loss = make_loss(self.n, displacement)
        self._loss = jax.jit(loss)
        self._grad = jax.jit(jax.grad(loss, has_aux=True))

    def _checked(self, f, x):
        out, nbrs = f(x, self.nbrs)
        if nbrs.did_buffer_overflow:  # host sync, as in jax-md's examples
            self.nbrs = self.neighbor_fn.allocate(x)
            out, nbrs = f(x, self.nbrs)
        self.nbrs = nbrs
        return out

    def loss(self, x):
        return self._checked(self._loss, x)

    def grad(self, x):
        return self._checked(self._grad, x)

title: 01. Particles: sort, cell lists, and data-dependent neighbour loops
text:
What this shows
Differentiating the irregular algorithm works. Enzyme differentiates the mutating, sort-based, data-dependent loop code directly and gets the same gradient as JAX and Reactant to machine precision. No padding, no capacity, no overflow check, no where tricks to keep sqrt finite. On the CPU at \(N = 10^6\), single-threaded Enzyme takes 4885.6 ms for the gradient, against 4575.5 ms for multithreaded JAX. The forward pass alone takes 1272.4 ms against 4042.6 ms.
Reactant behaves like JAX. Reactant is Julia, but compiled through XLA, and it needs the same regularisation: padded cells, masks, a branch-free kernel. Its gradient takes 70.8 ms against JAX’s 62.5 ms, even though its padded cell list evaluates 6× more pair slots than jax-md’s pre-filtered pair list. The constraint comes from the static-graph execution model, not from the language.

section: Where JAX wins / where Enzyme hurts
text:
Where JAX wins / where Enzyme hurts






WarningOn the GPU, today, JAX’s padded version is much faster than Enzyme’s



At \(N = 10^6\) the Enzyme GPU gradient takes 1053.1 ms, 194× its own forward pass. JAX takes 62.5 ms.
The reason is how Enzyme compiles reverse-mode GPU kernels with a data-dependent inner loop: it stores values for every inner iteration in device malloc memory, in both the augmented forward kernel and the reverse kernel. With CUDA’s default 8 MB device heap this crashes above about 30 000 particles, so the notebook raises the heap to 2 GiB. A branch-free kernel and a fixed-trip-count kernel showed the same behaviour.


What we did not do:

No hand-written adjoint on either side. A JAX expert could write the neighbour loop as a Pallas kernel with a hand-written backward pass. An Enzyme user could restructure the GPU gradient as a forward kernel plus a gather kernel that applies Enzyme only to the scalar pair function. Both are faster, and both give up “the adjoint for free”.
No multithreaded Enzyme CPU version. The CPU numbers are single-threaded Julia against multithreaded XLA.
jax-md’s capacity_multiplier left at 1.25, its default.

# Reactant traces Julia array code into one XLA program, so it has JAX's constraints:
# static shapes, no data-dependent loop bounds, no branches on traced values. The cell
# list is regularised like a padded JAX cell list: every neighbour cell is read
# through `cap` slots and slots past the cell's end are masked.

# `W` from common.jl branches (`if q < 1`), which cannot be traced. Select instead,
# evaluating both polynomials for every pair, as JAX's `jnp.where` does.
@inline function W_select(r, h::T) where {T}
    q = r / h
    σ = T(10) / (T(7) * T(π) * h * h)
    t = max(2 - q, zero(T))
    return σ * ifelse(q < 1, 1 - T(1.5) * q * q + T(0.75) * q * q * q, T(0.25) * t * t * t)
end

"""
First sorted index of each cell, using only sorts and gathers: merge the sorted cell
ids (keys 2c) with one probe per cell (keys 2c−1); the rank of probe c, minus the
c−1 probes before it, is the start of cell c.
"""
function cell_starts(cs, ncells)
    N = length(cs)
    probes = 2 .* Int32.(1:ncells+1) .- Int32(1)
    order = sortperm(vcat(2 .* cs, Reactant.promote_to(typeof(cs), probes)))
    rank = sortperm(order)                       # inverse permutation
    return rank[N+1:end] .- Int32.(0:ncells)
end

function sph_loss_padded(x::AbstractMatrix, p::Params{T}, ::Val{cap}) where {T,cap}
    N, nc = size(x, 2), p.nc
    s = p.L / nc

    cell = Int32(1) .+ mod.(floor.(Int32, x[1, :] ./ s), Int32(nc)) .+
           Int32(nc) .* mod.(floor.(Int32, x[2, :] ./ s), Int32(nc))
    perm = sortperm(cell)
    cs = cell[perm]
    start = cell_starts(cs, nc * nc)
    xs, ys = x[1, perm], x[2, perm]
    cxs, cys = (cs .- Int32(1)) .% Int32(nc), (cs .- Int32(1)) .÷ Int32(nc)
    slots = reshape(Int32.(0:cap-1), cap, 1)

    ρ = zero(xs)
    for dy in -1:1, dx in -1:1                   # unrolled at trace time
        cn = Int32(1) .+ mod.(cxs .+ Int32(dx), Int32(nc)) .+
             Int32(nc) .* mod.(cys .+ Int32(dy), Int32(nc))
        idx = reshape(start[cn], 1, N) .+ slots                  # (cap, N) candidates
        valid = idx .< reshape(start[cn .+ Int32(1)], 1, N)
        l = clamp.(idx, Int32(1), Int32(N))
        rx = minimg.(reshape(xs, 1, N) .- xs[l], p.L)
        ry = minimg.(reshape(ys, 1, N) .- ys[l], p.L)
        r2 = rx .^ 2 .+ ry .^ 2
        inside = valid .& (r2 .< 4 * p.h * p.h)
        r = sqrt.(ifelse.(inside, r2, one(T)))  # keep sqrt' finite on masked slots
        ρ = ρ .+ vec(sum(ifelse.(inside, p.m .* W_select.(r, p.h), zero(T)); dims=1))
    end
    return sum((ρ .- p.ρ0) .^ 2)
end

"Capacity needed: the largest cell occupancy. Too small silently drops neighbours."
function max_occupancy(x, p)
    s, nc = p.L / p.nc, p.nc
    counts = zeros(Int, nc * nc)
    for i in axes(x, 2)
        counts[1 + mod(floor(Int, x[1, i] / s), nc) + nc * mod(floor(Int, x[2, i] / s), nc)] += 1
    end
    return maximum(counts)
end

title: Methodology
text: How the comparisons are made, so they can be checked and reproduced.

title: Methodology
text:
Same inputs
Inputs for each example are generated once in Julia with a fixed seed and written to data/<example>.npz. All three implementations load that file.

title: Methodology
text:
Same gradient
Every implementation computes the gradient of the same loss at the same point in Float64 and saves it to benchmarks/grads/<example>_<impl>.npz. Each example page checks that

every gradient agrees with central finite differences on a few random components, and
all three gradients agree with each other (relative tolerance 1e-8).

A failing check fails the build, so a published page always shows matching gradients.

title: Methodology
text:
Timing

Timing runs use Float32, as is usual on GPUs; the correctness check uses Float64.
Compile time (first call) is reported separately from run time. It matters for JAX and Reactant, which compile a whole graph, and for Enzyme, which compiles on first call.
Run time is the median of 10 calls after 2 warm-up calls. GPU work is synchronised inside the timed region (CUDA.synchronize, jax.block_until_ready).
Problem size N is swept over several orders of magnitude so scaling is visible, not just one data point.
Peak device memory is reported where the tool exposes it.
Benchmarks run on an otherwise idle GPU (make gpu-check refuses to run otherwise).

title: Methodology
section: Fairness rules for the JAX column
text:
Fairness rules for the JAX column
The JAX code is what a competent JAX user would write, not a literal translation:

jax.jit everything, donate buffers where it helps, and use jax.checkpoint where a practitioner would.
Use the ecosystem’s own tools where they exist: jax-md cell and neighbour lists, Optimistix for implicit differentiation, Diffrax for adaptive time stepping.
Where JAX needs a static capacity (padding), size it from the data and handle overflow the way jax-md does, and report the padding overhead.
Every example page has a “Where JAX wins / what we did not do” note.

title: Methodology
text:
Hardware and software
Results on the published site were produced on an NVIDIA RTX 5000 Ada Generation Laptop GPU (16 GB), Julia 1.12, Enzyme.jl 0.13, Reactant.jl 0.2, JAX 0.11 (CUDA 13). Exact versions are pinned in julia/Manifest.toml and python/uv.lock.
